A quiche is a savory, baked dish that looks like an open pie. It has a crispy pastry shell on the bottom and sides, and is filled with a creamy, egg-based mixture that is baked until firm.
Breaking it down, piece by piece

1. It is a savory dish, not a sweet one.
When we say "savory," we mean it is not a dessert. It is eaten as a meal — for breakfast, lunch, brunch, or a light dinner. Even though it looks somewhat like a pie, it is not filled with fruit or sugar. It is more like a baked egg dish in a pastry shell.

2. The outer shell: the crust
The base of a quiche is a thin, buttery pastry crust — similar to a pie crust. This crust covers the bottom and the sides of the baking dish, forming a bowl-like shell that holds the filling inside. There is no pastry on top. The top is completely open, which is why a quiche is sometimes called an open-faced tart or open-faced pie. After baking, the crust turns golden, crisp, and slightly flaky.

3. The filling: the custard
The inside of a quiche is called the filling or the custard. This is what makes a quiche distinctive. The custard is made by whisking together eggs and cream (or milk) until smooth, and then pouring this mixture into the pastry shell. When this egg-and-cream mixture bakes in the oven, it transforms from a liquid into a soft, silky, slightly wobbly solid — almost like a very smooth, creamy egg cake. This texture is what people mean when they say quiche is "custardy."

4. The extra ingredients inside the filling
The egg-and-cream custard on its own is the base, but almost every quiche also has additional ingredients mixed into or layered within the custard. These can include:

  • Cheese (very common — Gruyère, cheddar, Swiss, etc.)
  • Cooked meats like bacon, ham, or smoked salmon
  • Vegetables like spinach, mushrooms, onions, caramelized leeks, or roasted peppers
  • Herbs and spices for flavor

These ingredients are arranged in the crust before the egg-cream mixture is poured over them, so they get embedded inside the custard as it bakes.
What does a quiche look like?

A quiche is almost always round, because it is baked in a round, shallow dish or tart tin. From the outside, it resembles a shallow pie. From a cross-section (if you cut a slice), you can clearly see two distinct layers: the thin golden-brown crust at the bottom and outer edges, and the thicker, creamy, pale-yellow custard filling above it. You may also see flecks of green from herbs or spinach, brown bits of bacon, or orange-yellow streaks from cheese running through the filling.

A quiche is typically sliced into wedge-shaped portions (like slices of a pie or pizza) and served either:

  • Hot or warm, fresh out of the oven
  • At room temperature, which is also perfectly acceptable and very common
  • Cold, especially for packed lunches, picnics, or leftovers

This flexibility — that it can be eaten at any temperature — is one reason quiche is so popular.
The most famous variety: Quiche Lorraine

The single most well-known type of quiche is called Quiche Lorraine. It contains bacon (or lardons — small cubes of cured pork) and Gruyère cheese mixed into the egg-and-cream custard. It is widely considered the "classic" quiche, and many other varieties are simply variations or adaptations of it.
Is a quiche hard to make at home?

Not particularly. The basic process involves:

  1. Pressing the pastry dough into a round tin to form the crust
  2. Placing the filling ingredients (like cheese or bacon) into the crust
  3. Pouring the egg-and-cream mixture over them
  4. Baking in an oven until the custard sets (becomes firm and no longer liquid)

The result is a complete, satisfying dish that works well as a main course, a party food, or even a snack.

A quiche is a round, savory baked dish with a crispy pastry shell and a soft, creamy egg-and-cream custard filling that typically includes cheese, meat, or vegetables — eaten as a meal, not a dessert.
